tweets: In 1819, a British officer chasing a tiger through the Deccan looked up at a cliff and froze — carved into the rock were 30 caves, painted 2,000 years ago, that no one alive remembered.

The caves at Ajanta were cut by Buddhist monks in two bursts of activity: one starting around the 2nd century BCE, another under Vakataka patronage around the 5th century CE. Then, sometime after, the site was abandoned and the jungle swallowed it whole.

Officer John Smith climbed up and stepped into what's now Cave 10 — walls covered in murals: Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives, princes, elephants, lotus pools, painted in pigments ground from rock, glue, and plant dye. He scratched his name into a pillar there.

For 13 centuries the paintings survived in the dark, sealed off by nothing but distance and silence. Ajanta is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the finest records of ancient Indian art on Earth. 🎨 Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
